For the first installment of the series, I would like to focus on, well, focus. Controlling the mind is a massive part of finding your path and self-transformation. The body and spirit need attention too, but I feel a lot of our modern world attacks the mind (purposely or not). Remember that even if your conscious mind doesn’t pick up on something, your subconscious mind is a sponge. I would like to focus most of this series on practices. Because I think we learn more by doing than reading. Life experience in invaluable.

Meditation – Meditation is simple to do, but difficult to explain properly, much like swimming. When you know how to swim, it's easier to show someone than to explain every little thing your body is doing. That being said, I wrote a guide but the advice can mostly be summed up as: Sit down and get comfortable in a chair/couch/floor. Relax your body so that there is no pain or discomfort distracting you. Close your eyes and attempt to clear your mind. Focus on your breath, every time a thought appears, simply observe the thought (don't get mad that you're thinking) and go back to your breath. Start with 5 minutes a day and see how you feel. Then increase the time if you want to challenge yourself.

Mindfulness – the opposite of mindlessness. We have all fallen into mindlessness and I would say most people do it almost all their waking hours. Driving a car, going for a walk, the bathroom, the shower, etc. How many of those things do you do while actively thinking about it? Do you often have concerns and worries darting back and forth through your mind? Mindfulness is the cure for this. My favorite is walking mindfulness aka walking meditation. Simply go for a walk and choose an object in the distance. It could be a tree, house, rock, etc. Say to yourself “I will be mindful while walking towards that.” Then, focus only on what you see, hear, feel, smell, and taste. Focus on your steps, your breath, the warmth of the air (or cold), the smell of the flowers, etc. This exercise is not limited to walking, but it is best done with something you enjoy or are ambivalent towards. It’s more difficult to be mindful in traffic, or when you’re in an office meeting, or hanging with the in-laws.

Accepting/Rejecting thoughts – This is a very simple exercise to not only help you control your thoughts, but also catch your mind from needlessly drifting. Whenever a thought you don’t like enters your mind simply say (aloud or in your mind) “I reject that thought”. The opposite is true as well, if something you like appears in your mind, say “I accept that thought”. This exercise is so very simple and becomes a great way of abjuring bad thoughts. Things this pertains to are negative future outcomes, self-doubt, worry, and stress.

Your word as Law – This may be the most difficult (arguably next to meditation) practice presented here. The practice is deceptively simple. Speak absolute truth. Now this doesn’t just pertain to raw honesty (which is a good practice on its own), but also promises you make. “I’m going to start eating better” can’t be followed with poor dietary habits. “I’m going to stop smoking” can’t be followed by smoking. In this exercise the focus is to change your words rather than the action. “I don’t eat well” and “I’m addicted to cigarettes” are more fitting for the above scenario. Even the phrase “I’m trying to lose weight” doesn’t hold any water if you don’t actively exercise or diet as well as you know you should. This practice is done so your word carries more weight. How many people do you disregard because they have lied to you in the past? Or they talk about how they want to "get their life together", but never actually do anything to accomplish this. You don't want to be that person.

This concludes my practices for controlling your mind. Adopt whichever you choose and see what works for you.
